en: A Direct Explanation of the *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra*, by the Ancient Wu Master O-yi, Zhi Xu. The explanation is divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the text. The explanation of the title is divided into three sections: first, the direct explanation of the treatise.
Title. Part two: identifying the author of the treatise. Part three: identifying the translator. Regarding the first [part]:

in the title *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra*, the two characters *nyāya* (inference/logic) refer to that which enters, and the two characters *praveśa* (entry) refer to that which is entered. As for "cause" (*hetu*), it refers to the [causes] of all phenomena...

Because it is ignited by this [reason], it constitutes one of the three members of a syllogism (*trirūpa-anumāna*). The three members refer to the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The thesis is not manifested without the reason, and the example is not established without the reason. Since the reason possesses the greatest power, it is designated as "Logic" (*Hetuvidyā*).

When the cause (*hetu*) is clarified, one is then able to establish [the correct] and able to refute [the erroneous]. Through refutation, there is nothing false that is not demolished; through establishment, there is nothing correct that is not revealed.

By demolishing the false, the self and phenomena of the parikalpita (imagined nature) are both destroyed; by revealing the correct, the true and conventional of the paratantra (dependent nature) and pariniṣpanna (perfected nature) stand together.
These two types of correct principles—the true and the conventional—are entered by means of *hetuvidyā* (logic); therefore, it is called "cause" (*hetu*).
This clarifies the entry into correct principle (*nyāya*). "Treatise" (*śāstra*) refers to that which is argued, elucidated, and adjudicated; it is of two kinds.

If it provides a detailed resolution of the scriptural text, it is called an *explanatory treatise* (*vyākhyā-śāstra*). If it establishes a doctrine based upon the scriptures, it is called a "treatise on tenets" (*siddhānta-śāstra*).
The present work is a treatise on tenets. II. Identifying the Author of the Treatise.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Śaṅkarapati.
This has not been seen translated previously. Some say it refers to the Lord of Heaven (Indra). "Bodhisattva" is explained as usual.
△ Third, the identification of the translator:
The Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty translated this work.
His life and deeds are recorded in the *Ci'en Zhuan*. To render the Sanskrit into Chinese is termed "translation" (*yi*). △ Second, the explanation.

The text consists of three parts: first, a summary of the essentials in verse; second, a detailed explanation of the eight sections; and third, a concluding summary in verse. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections:
first, the verse on the two benefits of the eight sections; second, the clarification of the inclusion of all essential meanings. This is the first [sub-section].

The means of proof (*sādhana*), the means of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), and their fallacies serve solely to enlighten others; direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and their fallacies serve solely for one's own enlightenment.
There is only one true means of proof, two true means of refutation, three fallacious means of proof, and four fallacious means of refutation. These constitute the four categories.

Causing others to attain awakening is collectively termed "benefiting others. Fifth is true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), sixth is true inference (*anumāna*), seventh is fallacious direct perception, and eighth is fallacious inference.
These four categories cause one to attain awakening for oneself and are collectively termed "benefiting oneself. Thus it is said: "eight gates and two benefits.
This constitutes the structural framework of this treatise; the subsequent text will explain it in detail, so there is no need for an elaborate commentary here. If...

Desiring to provide prior knowledge, I shall briefly set forth the general outline. A "true *sthāpanā*" (true establishment) refers to that which, being free from faults in its three members (*trirūpa*), can manifest the correct [view] and awaken others.
A "true *dūṣaṇa*" (true refutation) refers to that which exposes the faults of another, thereby crushing heterodoxy and enlightening the questioner.

A "pseudo-*sthāpanā*" (semblance of establishment) refers to that which, though intending to present a formal inference (*pramāṇa*), possesses faulty members and is thus insufficient to enlighten others. A "pseudo... [refutation].
Refutation: This refers to wishing to censure another by falsely attributing faults to them when they actually have no faults. True direct perception (*pratyakṣa*):

This refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) which realizes the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena. True inference (*anumāna*): This refers to the arising of correct knowledge by means of observing an object through its signs (*liṅga*).

That which resembles direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) refers to conceptual cognition that operates erroneously with respect to its object. That which resembles inference (*anumāna*) refers to false discrimination that cannot correctly understand [the object].
Question: When one establishes the true and refutes the true, one can thereby awaken others; however, when one establishes the semblance and refutes the semblance, how can this lead to awakening?
What is meant by "awakening others"? It refers to true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and true inference (*anumāna*), by which one may awaken oneself.

What are false direct perception and false inference? How does one awaken oneself? The answer is: the four truths are the medicine, while the four semblances are the disease. If one does not recognize the disease, one will not know the medicine.

Therefore, each of the eight gates must be individually examined. These constitute the means of establishment (*sādhana*) and the means of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), as well as true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and true inference (*anumāna*), all of which are termed *hetuvidyā* (the science of logic).
Self-awakening and awakening others are both termed "entry" (*praveśa*). The four fallacies and that which is to be refuted are erroneous;
that which is established, that which is observed, and that which is revealed are the correct principles (*nyāya*). II. Explaining the Subsumption of All Essential Meanings.
Thus, the essential meaning of all treatises is summarized:
namely, these eight gates and two benefits. Not only do they encompass this single treatise, but they have already summarized the essential meaning of all treatises.

For although the meanings of treatises are numerous, the establishment of their chapters does not go beyond the two gates of refutation and proof; and the convergence upon principle does not exceed [the aforementioned].
This brings forth the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate; for the benefit [of others] does not, in total, transcend the two awakenings of self and other.
II. Detailed Explanation of the Eight Gates, Divided into Seven: 1. The Gate of the Authentic Means of Proof (*sādhana*). 2. The Gate of the Fallacious Means of Proof. 3.

The Two Gates of Authentic Direct Perception (*pratyakṣa*) and Authentic Inference (*anumāna*). 4. The Gate of Fallacious Direct Perception. 5. The Gate of Fallacious Inference. 6. The Gate of the Authentic Means of Refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).
Section on the Gates. Seven: The Gate of the Counterfeit Refutation. Question: This explanation of the eight gates differs from the sequence in the verse;
why is this? Answer: The verse lists the eight gates based on two benefits, which was done for the sake of literary convenience.

This explanation of the eight gates intends for one to enter contemplation according to the text in order to accomplish the two benefits of self-benefit and benefit for others. Why is this? Because of the Truth...
The ability to establish [the thesis] gives rise to correct understanding; by means of what appears to be an establishment, one guards against erroneous understanding.

Once understanding is perfected, one enters into realization, attaining true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and true inference (*anumāna*), which are precisely the two wisdoms of the fundamental and the subsequently attained.

Only through the realization of these two wisdoms does one come to know the falsity of what merely appears to be direct perception and inference; therefore, it is only when one has truly attained these two wisdoms that one is able to refute and establish.

To cause others to attain realization—if one’s discourse resembles what is fallacious for direct perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) or inference (*anumānābhāsa*), it merely results in a semblance of refutation and a semblance of proof.

How can one not be cautious? First, the section on the genuine means of proof (*samyag-sādhana*), which has three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation; third, the conclusion. Now, the first [the heading]:

In this context, the multiple statements consisting of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth are termed the "proof" (*sādhana*). This is because, by means of these multiple statements—the thesis, the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—the meaning that remains uncomprehended by those who inquire is revealed.

This means that within this section, the various linguistic expressions consisting of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are called "the proof" (*sādhana*). Why is this?
Because by means of these various linguistic expressions—the thesis, the reason, and the example—one is able to reveal the meaning that has not yet been understood by those who raise questions.

The second part, the explanation, is further divided into three sections: first, the explanation of the thesis; second, the explanation of the reason; and third, the explanation of the example. Now, the first [of these].

In this context, a "thesis" (*pakṣa*) refers to a property-bearer (*dharmin*) that is generally recognized and a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) that is generally recognized, which, by virtue of their distinct nature, are intended by oneself to be established as the probandum (*sādhya*). This is called a thesis. For example: "Sound is impermanent."
Regarding this gate of the true proof (*sādhana*), among the three members [of a syllogism], that which is called the "thesis" (*pakṣa*) consists of:
the subject (*dharmin*) established by common consensus as the basis of the thesis; the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) established by common consensus as the essence of the thesis;
and the specific nature intended by one's own mind. For these reasons, it is called a "thesis. To state it briefly: it is simply according to one's own intention.
That which is intended to be established is called the thesis (*pakṣa*). For example, when someone establishes that "sound is impermanent," they cite one instance as an illustration for all others.
Whatever is established, provided it does not contradict reason, constitutes a genuine, validly established thesis.
The word "sound" is the subject (*dharmin*) presented first; the two characters "impermanence" constitute the essence of the thesis (*sādhya*) presented subsequently.
One may point specifically to the sound of a treatise as being impermanent, or point to other sounds as being impermanent, or point generally to all sounds as being impermanent.
Although not spoken by the mouth, there is that which is pointed to by the mind; this is precisely what is meant by "intentional admission of a specific distinction."
"Extremely established" (*prasiddha*) means that it is definitively accomplished through reasoning, such that there is no fault of mutual non-acceptance.
"Subject" (*dharmin*) means it is not merely a name like "tortoise hair" or "rabbit horns. "The qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) is precisely the essence of the thesis (*pakṣa*);

it is stated to clarify that the subject of the prior member (*pūrvapakṣa*) is the basis of the thesis, as it is that which is to be qualified. [This excludes] the two views of eternalism and nihilism.

Both of these are merely the conceptual constructs of non-Buddhists. To now speak of "impermanence" is to refute the view of eternalism; yet in reality, it is neither truly eternal nor subject to annihilation.
This is thus the authentic seal of the Hīnayāna and the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna; for this reason, this single school is cited here.

This briefly demonstrates the proof (*sādhana*). Now, although the three realms—including both the environment and its inhabitants—are entirely impermanent, sound alone is singled out here because the sense-object of sound perishes as soon as it arises and cannot endure for even a moment; thus, the meaning of impermanence is most easily demonstrated by it.
If one knows that sound is impermanent, one can then understand by analogy that all things are impermanent. Since all are impermanent, they are also certainly...

"Non-self. Is this not the essential key for revealing the two types of emptiness? Furthermore, since both the *Śābarabhāṣya* and the *Śabdanityatādhikaraṇa* maintain that sound is eternal, one establishes against them that sound is impermanent.
II. Explaining the Reason (hetu) has three parts: first, a general presentation of the three characteristics;
second, a detailed explanation of the two categories; third, concluding with the nature of the reason. Now, the first.

The reason (*hetu*) has three characteristics. What are these three? They are: (1) being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), (2) being necessarily present in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattvam*), and (3) being entirely absent in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣe 'sattvam*).
"Reason" (*hetu*) means that by which something is derived; it is the ground [of inference]. For example, whatever is produced is necessarily impermanent. Therefore...
The three characters "produced" (*kṛtaka*) serve as the reason (*hetu*) for the basis and the ground, establishing the thesis (*pakṣa*) of impermanence as its result.
This single reason possesses three characteristics (*trirūpa*) in relation to the thesis and the example:
first, it must necessarily be pervasive throughout the thesis and the nature of the subject (*dharmin*), such as the three characters "produced" in relation to sound.

This has its own rule: the thesis of impermanence is definitively characterized by the sense of having a produced nature; therefore, it is called "the property of being a reason that is coextensive with the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*).
Taking one instance as an illustration for all others, whatever reason is put forward must not contradict the property of the subject.
Second, within the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), there must be the nature of necessary presence. For example, "impermanence" in the case of a jar and so forth is called a similar instance;
it necessarily possesses the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*). Third, within the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), there must be the nature of universal absence.
For example, "space and so forth are not impermanent" is called a dissimilar instance; this refers to the exhaustive investigation [of its absence].
This seeks to definitively establish the meaning of the nature of non-action. △ Second, the separate explanation of the two categories.
What are called the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)? That which possesses the same logical meaning as the property to be established is called the similar class.

For example, when establishing impermanence: "A jar and so forth are impermanent" is called the similar instance (*sapakṣa*). As for the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), it refers to a place where that which is to be established does not exist;
for example, if something were permanent, one would observe that it is not produced, such as space and so forth.
Regarding the term "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*): it refers to a category that is equal and equivalent to the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) being established.

For example, when "impermanence" is established as the thesis, and jars and the like are impermanent, these are called similar examples (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*). Regarding the term "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*):
it refers to a location where, within the dissimilar example, the thesis of impermanence established by oneself is absent; this is called a dissimilar example (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*). That is to say:
If there were such a thing as permanence, it would be seen as non-produced, like space and so forth. If there is the thesis-term "permanence," it excludes the position of "impermanence.
If there is the term "non-produced," it excludes the reason of "being produced. Terms such as "like space" serve as counter-examples to "like a jar" and so forth;

therefore, the preceding text states that [the reason] is entirely absent from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). Nāgārjuna said: "If that which is to be established does not exist, there can be no statement [of it]."

This is called the "dissimilar class" (*vipakṣa*). It is not merely that which is contrary to or different from the similar class (*sapakṣa*). △ Third, the conclusion establishing the nature of the reason:

here, the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) or the property of being produced immediately following volitional effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) that pervades [the entire subject] and exists within the similar class.
The presence of the property in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) and its universal absence in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣe 'tyantābhāvaḥ*) constitute the reason for impermanence and so forth.
That is to say, for example, if one establishes the thesis that "sound is impermanent," and takes either "being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*) as the reason,
or "being produced by volitional effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatvāt*) as the reason, then [the reason] is universally...

The nature of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the property-to-be-proven (*dharma*) is both "certainly present in similar instances" (*sapakṣe sattvam*) and "entirely absent in dissimilar instances" (*vipakṣe 'sattvam*).
Therefore, it can serve as the reason (*hetu*) for the thesis of impermanence, as well as for its similar and dissimilar examples. Regarding the two reasons cited in the text:

the reason of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is explained in contrast to the *Abhidharmadīpa*, while the reason of "being produced by volitional effort without interval" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is explained in contrast to the *Nyāyapraveśaka*.
The Reason (*hetu*). In response to the proponents of the Manifestation Theory (*abhivyaktivādin*):

△ Third, the explanation of the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*). There are two kinds of analogies: first, the analogy by similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*); second, the analogy by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Regarding the analogy by similarity:

it is that instance where the presence of the reason is shown to be invariably present in the similar class (*sapakṣa*). That is to say: "Whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, such as a jar, for example. Dissimilar... [text fragment]

Regarding the method (*nyāya*): when it is stated that at a certain locus the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent because the reason (*hetu*) is entirely non-existent—namely, if something were eternal (*nitya*), one would see that it is not produced (*akṛtaka*), as in the case of space and so forth—here the word "eternal" indicates that it is not impermanent (*anitya*), and the phrase "not produced" indicates that there is no production.
Just as with existence and non-existence, this is called "non-existence."
First, there is the dual presentation; next, each is explained individually. First, regarding the explanation of the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*):

if, in the context of this example, it is demonstrated that the reason is definitely present in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), that is to say, if the reason of being produced is seen to exist in the thesis of impermanence.
Thus, one uses things such as a jar as a positive example (*sapakṣa*). Since a jar is also produced and a jar is also impermanent, it is called a "similar instance" (*sādharmya*).

Next, the explanation of the negative instance (*vipakṣa*) has two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the exclusion of non-examples. First, regarding the formal explanation of the negative instance:
if, in the case of this example, the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*) is definitely absent, [it is a negative instance].
The absence of the nature of the probans (*hetu*) throughout [the dissimilar instances] is what is called the "dissimilar instance" (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

That is to say, if something were eternal, it would lack the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) that is impermanent; seeing that it is not produced, it lacks the nature of the probans which is being produced throughout.

For example, in the case of space and so forth, there are no jars or similar things to serve as a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*); therefore, it is called the "dissimilar instance. Next, this is further distinguished from what is not [the correct dissimilar instance].
What is meant here by "permanent" (nitya) is merely intended to indicate that which is not impermanent; it does not establish "permanence" as a thesis (pakṣa) in opposition to "impermanence.
What is meant here by "not produced" (akṛtaka) is merely intended to indicate that which is unproduced;
it does not establish "non-produced-ness" as a reason (hetu) in opposition to "the produced" (kṛtaka).
It is so. For example, "non-existence" (abhāva) is not itself an existent thing; it is merely called "non-existence" because it is the negation of existence.
How could one say that there is yet another entity called "non-existence" that stands in opposition to existence?

This precisely demonstrates that we merely borrow the analogy of space—which is eternally non-active—to serve as a counter-example, in order to manifest the primary thesis of impermanence. It certainly does not establish space as [an ultimate reality].
This is the eternal principle (*nitya*). If one calculates that space (*ākāśa*) is definitively existent and definitively eternal, this is precisely the view of a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*).
The above concludes the first section, "The Gate of the True Proof," consisting of the initial proposition and its two-fold explanation. △ Third, the conclusion.
It has already been stated that when such multiple statements as the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and so forth, are used to enlighten another, they are called the "proof" (*sādhana*).

For example, the statement "Sound is impermanent" is the statement of the thesis. The statement "Because it is a product" (*kṛtakatvāt*) is the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

The statement "If something is a product, it is seen to be impermanent, like a jar and so forth" is the statement of the concordant instance (*sapakṣānugama*). The statement "If it were eternal, it would not be a product" is... [the statement of the dissimilar instance].
To "act like space" is a term for being free from verbal expression. Only these three components are designated as the "proof" (*sādhana*).
The three members have already been explained at length; now they shall be summarized and presented collectively.

This refers to the various linguistic formulations of the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) mentioned above, which, when used to enlighten others, are called the proof. Furthermore, if—

To say "sound is impermanent" is the statement that establishes the thesis (*pakṣa*). To say "because it is produced" is the statement that the reason (*hetu*) is entirely a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
To combine these by saying "whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, like a jar and so forth," is the statement of its presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
To say "even if it were permanent, it would not be [produced]" is the statement of its absence from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).
The phrase "that which is produced is like space" is precisely a statement that distances itself from the thesis of impermanence and the reason of being produced.
It is only these three members—the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—that are designated as the "proof" (*sādhana*).

Within this context, the fact that the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is merely called a "statement of distancing" correctly demonstrates that it is simply a negation of the similar property (*sādharmya*); it does not imply the establishment of a further thesis of permanence.

And it is also not a *kāryahetu* (effect-reason). Question: In the statement regarding "conformity with similar instances" (*anvaya*), why is it first said, "If it were something produced," and then followed by, "One perceives its impermanence"?
In the statement regarding "exclusion from dissimilar instances" (*vyatireka*), why is it first said, "If it were eternal," and then followed by, "One perceives that it is not something produced"?
Answer: One could simply say that all things of the nature of being produced are...

Regarding impermanence, one cannot state that "whatever is impermanent is necessarily a product. This is why, in a formal application (*upanaya*), the reason must necessarily precede the thesis (*pakṣa*).
However, one may state that "if something is permanent, it is certainly not a product," but one cannot state that "whatever is not a product is necessarily permanent.
This is why, in a formal exclusion (*vyatireka*), the thesis must necessarily precede the reason.
This is the cause. The first section, "The Gate of Genuine *sādhana*," is concluded. △ Second, "The Gate of Fallacious *sādhana*" has two parts:

first, the actual explanation; second, the summary of faults. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the explanation of fallacious propositions (*pakṣābhāsa*); second, the explanation of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*); third, the explanation of fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).

Within the first of these, there are again three subsections: first, the enumeration of the nine fallacies; second, the individual explanation of the nine fallacies; third, the summary of the nine fallacies. Now, the first [subsection].

Although they may appear to establish [a thesis], because they contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, they are called "pseudo-theses" (not true proofs). That is to say: contradiction with direct perception;

contradiction with inference (*anumāna*); contradiction with one's own scriptures (*āgama*); contradiction with worldly consensus; contradiction with one's own words; the unestablished nature of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-aprasiddha*);
the unestablished nature of the qualified (*viśeṣya-aprasiddha*); the unestablished nature of both; and that which is already established by consensus (*prasiddha-anuvāda*).
The following text explains this itself; there is no need for further interpretation. I shall merely set forth the general meaning.

*Pratyakṣa* (direct perception) refers to that which is known by non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). *Anumāna* (inference) refers to that which is known by correct conceptualizing wisdom (*samyag-vikalpa-jñāna*).

*Svāgama* (one’s own scripture) refers to the teachings each has received, whether Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, internal or external schools. *Loka* (the world) refers to that upon which worldly people rely.

Regarding matters commonly accepted within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are five types of contradictions with one's own words—namely, the thesis (*pakṣa*) as established by oneself.
If any one of these five is contradicted, it is not a truly valid establishment of a thesis. The "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) refers to the latter member, the essence of the thesis;

the "qualified" (*viśeṣya*) refers to the former member, the factual base (*dharmin*). "Both" refers to the thesis and the factual base together. If either of these two is [contradicted], [it likewise fails to be a valid thesis].

If [the reason] itself is not established, it cannot establish [the thesis]; how much less so when both are unestablished? How could it possibly establish anything? "Conformity" (sādharmya-sama) means that there is no further distinction between oneself and the opponent.

Since they have already reached a common ground, what need is there to establish it separately? For this reason, it is also called a "pseudo-thesis" (pratijñābhāsa), as it is not a genuine means of establishment.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the nine fallacies.
Among these, contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is as follows: for example, to say that sound is not audible.
The auditory consciousness hears sound, and this is an object of direct perception; for sound is the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the auditory consciousness.

When the auditory consciousness directly hears sound, it does not carry names or phrases (*nāma-pada*), because it is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*). If one were to establish "non-[audibility]" as a predicate (*dharma*) of the subject (*dharmin*) "sound," [it would contradict direct perception].
The tenets one hears thus contradict the principles of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
As for contradiction with inference (*anumāna*), it is as when one says that jars and the like are permanent;
although jars are currently manifest, they must ultimately be impermanent. This is precisely what is known through inferential cognition (*paricchedaka-jñāna*). If...
To establish the thesis that phenomena such as jars are permanent contradicts the principles known through inference (*anumāna*).
As for contradiction with one’s own teachings (*svaśāstravirodha*), it is, for example, like the Vaiśeṣika masters establishing sound as permanent.
The Vaiśeṣika masters establish six categories (padārtha): first, substance; second, quality; third, action; fourth, great existence; fifth, sameness and difference; and sixth, inherence.
Within the second category, that of quality, there are twenty-four types; sound is now one among these twenty-four.
Thus, according to their own school’s doctrine, they also maintain that sound is subsumed under the category of quality. This is simply because...
That which has the nature of being produced is not eternal in its essence. For example, if one were to further establish sound as eternal, it would contradict one's own doctrine.
As for contradiction with the world, it is like saying that the hare in the moon does not exist there; or again, it is like saying that human skull-bones [are pure].
It is impure because it belongs to the category of sentient beings, just like a conch shell.
That a rabbit becomes pregnant by gazing at the moon, and that the human skull is impure—these are all things known to the world.
Now, if one were to say that a mother rabbit conceives a young rabbit not by gazing at the moon, or alternatively, if one were to say...
The human skull is pure because it is a part of a sentient being’s body; it is, for example, like a conch shell.
This, however, contradicts worldly convention. One should understand that the reason it is a part of a sentient being is illustrated by the analogy of the conch shell.
In all such cases, one can establish the thesis of impurity, but it is impossible to establish a thesis of purity.
An instance of self-contradiction is, for example, saying, "My mother is a barren woman."
One who gives birth to my body is called my mother. A barren woman cannot give birth to a child;
were one to claim that one's mother is a barren woman, it would contradict one's own words.

Regarding the case where the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is not established for the opponent: it is like a follower of the Buddha establishing the "destruction" (*vināśa*) of sound against a Sāṃkhya teacher.
The "qualifier" refers to the predicate of the thesis (*pakṣa*). In this context, the two characters "destruction" (*vināśa*) are such [a qualifier].

Sound is inherently momentary and subject to destruction; however, the Sāṃkhya teacher absolutely does not admit that sound is destroyed. Therefore, one establishes its destruction in relation to him.
The thesis (pakṣa) is called "unestablished" because the opponent is absolutely unwilling to accept it.

If one wishes to refute the Sāṃkhya teacher’s position that sound is a real entity, one should state: "Sound is the subject (dharmin); it is definitely not a real entity" is the thesis (pakṣa). The reason (hetu) is: [as follows].
Because the three factors are combined, they serve as a common analogy, such as an army or a forest; the refutation of the doctrine of permanence is likewise.

This is explained in detail in the first fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. As for the "three factors," according to the Sāṃkhya school’s calculations, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* constitute the means of production (*sādhana*), while the twenty-three principles constitute that which is produced (*sādhya*). Sound, however, is one of those [twenty-three] calculated [principles].
This is one of the three [requirements of a thesis].

Regarding "that which is to be distinguished" (*viśeṣya*) not being established: for example, when a Sāṃkhya teacher says to a Buddhist disciple, "The self (*ātman*) is volition (*cetanā*)," the "self" refers to the subject (*dharmin*) previously presented; this is what the word "self" here denotes. A Buddhist disciple would certainly never...

It is granted that the self may be established as an existent phenomenon; therefore, to say in this context that "the self is volition" is not an unestablished claim, because the disciples of the Buddha definitively know that there is no self.
Regarding that which is not established for both parties: for example, when a Vaiśeṣika teacher posits a self (*ātman*) as the cause of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) for a Buddhist disciple,

the Vaiśeṣika considers the self to be subsumed under the category of substance (*dravya-padārtha*), because of its qualities (*guṇa-padārtha*) such as cognition (*buddhi*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and effort (*prayatna*).
The ninefold causes and conditions of the conjunction—namely, courage, conduct, dharma, and non-dharma—are able to give rise to the characteristic of cognition, which is called the "self.

Because the self acts as the causal condition for the phrase of conjunction, and because the phrase of conjunction causes the nine qualities to conjoin with the self to give rise to the characteristic of cognition, the conjunction and the cognition it gives rise to are cited to manifest the essence of the self. However, the disciples of the Buddha...
If a real self is not admitted, then their establishment of a self as the "distinguished" (viśeṣya) would not be fully established.

Since the disciples of the Buddha do not admit that a composite entity (*saṃghāta-pada*) exists substantially, then their establishment of the causes and conditions of the composite as the "distinguisher" (*viśeṣaṇa*) [would likewise not be established].
Nor is it universally established; therefore, it is said that both are not universally established.

These causes and conditions of conjunction are the falsely imagined external real dharmas outside of the mind by the Vaiśeṣika non-Buddhists; they are erroneous causes and conditions, not the twelve links of dependent origination within the True Teaching.
Regarding "concordant consensus" (*siddhasādhana*): for example, when it is said that sound is audible, everyone knows that sound is audible.
Since both parties already agree on this, what need is there to laboriously formulate a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to debate it?
Therefore, the root treatise states: "If, as in the case of 'sound,' both meanings are equally accepted, neither need be stated. This refers to the meaning.
If there were a contradiction, one would necessarily have to establish a formal inference (*pramāṇa*). Since the two now accord with one another, there is no need to state it further.

To state what should not be stated is merely a superfluous matter; therefore, it constitutes a fault. This concludes the second section: the detailed explanation of the nine faults. △ Third, the summary of the nine faults.

Such excessive verbiage constitutes a fallacy of the thesis (pratijñā-doṣa) because it excludes the door of the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of all phenomena, fails to establish [the intended meaning],
and renders the formulation fruitless.

"Many words" refers to the nine types of pseudo-theses (*pakṣābhāsa*) mentioned above. "To refute" means to contradict. The first five fallacies of contradiction (*virodha*) involve the exclusion of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena;

the latter three—the fallacies of non-establishment (*asiddha*), contradiction with what is already established (*pratītibādhita*), and establishment by what is already established (*prasiddhabādhita*)—are such that their establishment is impossible.
These nine types of pseudo-theses are established because, in total, they do not produce the fruit of knowledge (*jñānaphala*). Regarding the [text]: "The... [the ellipsis indicates the conclusion].
This cannot be called a true *sādhana* (proof). Regarding the method of negating the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena:
for example, to say that "sound is not audible" directly contradicts the specific characteristic of sound by means of this very statement "not audible. It is like saying "a jar is permanent."
This very term "permanent" contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a jar;

just as establishing sound as permanent contradicts the specific characteristic of sound, so too saying that the hare-bearing [sky] is not the moon contradicts the specific characteristic of the hare.
Likewise, saying that human skull-bone is pure contradicts the specific characteristic of the skull-bone itself. This very term "pure" thus contradicts the specific characteristic of the skull-bone.
It is contradictory. For example, to say "my mother is a barren woman" is for the very term "barren woman" to contradict itself as applied to my own mother.
That which cannot be established refers to the three types of non-establishment (*asiddha*); since these are not accepted by the opponent, they cannot be established.
That which is established through mutual agreement (*prasiddha*) leaves nothing to be disputed; therefore, there is no need to falsely posit it, nor can it be established [in that manner].

[The section on] "Establishment" is concluded. Regarding "that which lacks a result": because a true *sādhana* (probative factor) causes one to give rise to correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), it is said to possess a result.
Now, as for a fallacious *sādhana*, since correct knowledge does not arise, it is without a result. △ Second, explaining the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
This has two parts: first, the general heading; second, the detailed explanation. Now, the first part.

The fallacious theses (*pratijñābhāsa*) have already been explained; now the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) shall be explained. Non-establishment (*asiddha*), inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*), and contradiction (*viruddha*) are termed fallacious reasons.
The four types of non-establishment, the six types of inconclusiveness, and the four types of contradiction are all called fallacious reasons; they are not true reasons that can establish a thesis.
Part Two: Detailed Explanation (in three sections): First, the explanation of non-establishment; second, the explanation of inconclusiveness; third, the explanation of contradiction.
[This section consists of] contradictions; it has two parts: first, the enumeration of names; second, the explanation of their characteristics. Now, for the first:

there are four types of non-establishment (*asiddha*): first, non-establishment for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*); second, non-establishment for one of the two (*anyatarāsiddha*); third, non-establishment through doubt (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*); and fourth, non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).
△ Second, the explanation of the characteristics [of the fallacies].
For example, in establishing sound as impermanent and so forth: if one says, "Because it has the nature of being visible to the eye," this is unestablished for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*).
Because of the reason "being a product" (*kṛtakatva*), it is unestablished for at least one party (*anyatarāsiddha*) when directed against the Proponent of Manifestation (*abhivyaktivādin*).
This first explains the first two types among the four kinds of "unestablished" (*asiddha*) reasons. To set up a formal argument (*pramāṇa*), one might say: "Sound is the subject (*dharmin*);
its impermanence is the thesis (*sādhya*). The reason (*hetu*) is: 'because it has the nature of being visible to the eye.

Since this is not accepted by either the proponent or the opponent, it is called "unestablished for both parties" (*ubhayāsiddha*). To set up another formal argument: "Sound is the subject; its impermanence is the thesis..."
Thesis: [Sound is eternal]. Reason: Because it is a product (*kṛtakatva*). If this is argued in opposition to the *Vyākaraṇa* (Grammar) school, it may be established;

however, if it is argued in opposition to the *Śabdābhivyaktivāda* (Theory of Sound Manifestation), the opponent will not accept it. Therefore, this is called "unestablished for one party" (*anyatarāsiddha*).

Regarding the term "Vyākaraṇa," there are those who dogmatically cling to the *Śabda-vidyā* (Science of Phonology) among the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) as being eternal, asserting that it can provide definitive certainty.

Since the *Yīnguǐ* (Measure of the *Yì*) uses [the nature of] measure to express and explain all phenomena, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* refutes it by asserting that it is a signifier (*vācaka*).

That is to say, other sounds are also capable of expressing meaning; since they are not eternal, how can the signifier of the *Śabdabrahma* (Sound-Theory) alone be eternal when it is identical to other sounds?
Now, one may likewise refute it on the grounds that it is a product (*kṛtaka*). Indeed, this is the case for the Sound-Theory.
Since it is something produced, it is necessarily impermanent. Regarding those who advocate the theory of sound-manifestation (*śabdābhivyakti-vāda*):
there are those who maintain that the nature of all sounds is eternally existent and not produced from conditions; rather, they only become expressive once manifested by external conditions.
For this reason, it is called the theory of sound-manifestation. In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this view is refuted on the grounds that [sounds] depend upon various conditions.
That is to say, since it depends upon various conditions—just like a jar or a garment—it is certainly not eternal.

Now, if one were to establish the reason "because it is a product" (*kṛtakatva*) against such a position, the opponent would counter-attack by saying: "Sound is something manifested (*vyakta*); how could it be a product?"

In that case, the opponent would not grant it; thus, the offense would be incomplete for either party. Therefore, if one is addressing the Śābda-vidhi-vādin (the Proponents of Manifestation through Sound), one must state:

"Because it is of a nature produced immediately following volitional effort. This is identical in meaning to the principle in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) regarding "depending upon various conditions.
However, if one were to address the Prābhākara school by means of the phrase "produced immediately following volitional effort," then for the Prābhākara...

This is not permitted; it also constitutes a violation of any one of the [required] conditions for non-establishment. This is why the two reasons were presented together within the "true proof" (*sādhana*) in the preceding text;
the intent lies herein, and one must not fail to understand this.
When doubt arises regarding the nature of mist and the like, one speaks of the existence of fire as a combination of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) in order to establish [the point];
however, such hesitation does not constitute proof.
This explains the third type of non-establishment (*asiddha*). To speak falsely because the realization of the principle is not yet certain is termed "hesitation" (*vimarśa*).
For example, when one sees mist rising from afar, though it is not actually smoke, one suspects it is smoke.

Consequently, in order to establish the thesis that fire exists through the combination of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), one might say: "The fire arising in the distance is a subject (*dharmin*) that possesses the property [of being smoke]."
The thesis is that fire is conjoined with the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). The reason (*hetu*) given is "because smoke is seen.

This, however, is a reason characterized by doubt and uncertainty; how could it establish the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)? By "primary elements," one refers to material, obstructive objects such as fuel and charcoal.
"Space is substantially existent because it is the basis for qualities (*guṇa*). Against those who argue that space is non-existent, this [argument] fails to establish a basis.

This explains the fourth "unestablished" (*asiddha*) reason. Space is not a real entity external to the mind; fundamentally, it cannot be determined as either definitively existent or definitively non-existent.
Nevertheless, there are non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who reckon space to be definitively existent, and others who reckon space to be definitively non-existent. Now...
Because it uses a reason that establishes definite existence to counter an argument that establishes definite non-existence, it is called the "unestablished basis" (*āśrayāsiddha*).
The proponent of definite existence says: "Space is an existent entity; its definite existence is the thesis. The reason is stated as: "Because it is the substratum of qualities.
This means that all things arise depending upon space and all abide depending upon space. The proponent of definite non-existence refutes this:

It is said: Because it is devoid of any substance, it is called "empty space. Since empty space does not exist, how can it serve as a basis? Thus, the reason—that it is the substratum for those qualities—is unestablished.
This concludes the fourfold explanation of the "unestablished" (*asiddha*) fallacy. △ Second, the explanation of the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) fallacy has two parts:
first, listing the names; second, explaining their characteristics. Now, the first [listing the names]:
There are six types of inconclusive [reasons]: first, the common; second, the uncommon; third, that which occurs in a portion of the similar class but pervades the dissimilar class;
fourth, that which occurs in a portion of the dissimilar class but pervades the similar class; fifth, that which occurs in a portion of both classes; and sixth, the contradictory certainty.
△ Second, the explanation of the characteristics.

Regarding "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) among these: for example, if one says, "Sound is eternal, because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatva*)," this reason is common to both the class of the eternal and the class of the non-eternal;
therefore, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Is sound non-eternal because it is an object of cognition like a jar, or is it [eternal] like space?
Because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), sound is eternal.

That is to say, for example, if one were to formulate a syllogism as follows: "Sound" is the subject (*dharmin*); "it is certainly eternal" is the thesis (*pakṣa*); "because it is an object of cognition" is the reason (*hetu*).
In this case, both the category of the eternal and the category of the non-eternal share this same reason; therefore, it is called the fallacy of the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*). Now...
One should counter-ask him: "Is sound impermanent like a jar because it possesses the nature of being an object of cognition?
Or is sound permanent like space because it possesses the nature of being an object of cognition?"
Regarding the term "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*): for example, it is said that sound is permanent because it possesses the nature of being audible.

Since both the category of the permanent and the category of the impermanent are devoid of this reason, and since nothing else exists outside of the permanent and the impermanent, this is a reason for doubt (*saṃśaya-hetu*). Of what sort is this "nature of being audible"?
This refers, for example, to formulating a syllogism as follows: "Sound is the subject; its permanence is the thesis; the reason is 'because it has the nature of being audible.

In this case, both the class of permanent things and the class of impermanent things are equally excluded from this reason; therefore, it is also called the fallacy of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

If the example is "like space," how can space be audible such that it would demonstrate permanence? If the example is "like a jar," how can a jar be audible [such that it would demonstrate impermanence]?

This demonstrates impermanence. Since there exists no other similar instance (*sapakṣa*) apart from the permanence of space and the impermanence of the jar, this would consequently become a reason of doubt (*anaikāntika-hetu*).
As for this property of being audible, it is neither permanent like space nor impermanent like a jar; ultimately, what could it possibly resemble?

Regarding "that which occurs in one part of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and occurs universally in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*"): for example, it is said, "Sound is not produced immediately following volitional effort, because it is impermanent.
In this case, the thesis (*pakṣa*)—"not produced immediately following volitional effort"—has lightning and space as its similar class (*sapakṣa*).
This property of impermanence exists in lightning and so forth, but does not exist in space and so forth. [It is] not produced immediately following volitional effort...

Establishing the thesis: taking jars and the like as the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), this reason is present in all of them. Since this reason takes both lightning and jars as its similar instances (*sapakṣa*), it is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For instance, just as jars and the like are impermanent and are produced through immediate effort (*puruṣaprayatna*), so too is lightning;
yet, just as lightning is impermanent and is not produced through immediate effort, so too are jars and the like. Thus, it is uncertain whether they are produced through immediate effort or not.
That is to say, for example, if one were to formulate a syllogism as follows: "Sound is the subject; its thesis is that it is not produced by effort and immediate [causation];
the reason is that it possesses the nature of impermanence. This reason of "the nature of impermanence" occurs only partially within the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Because it occurs pervasively in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), it is also termed the "inconclusive fallacy" (*anaikāntika-doṣa*).

For in this context, since the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that [sound] is not produced by immediate effort (*aprayatnānantarīyaka*), lightning, space, and so forth should serve as the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
However, while this reason—the property of impermanence—is present in lightning and the like, it is absent in space and the like.

This [reason] occurs partially within the similar class (*sapakṣa*). Furthermore, since this thesis—that [sound] is not produced by effort (*aprayatnāntarīyaka*)—should take jars and the like as its dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), yet this reason of "impermanence" actually exists pervasively in those jars and so forth;
thus, it occurs pervasively within the dissimilar class. The formal refutation above is concluded. Below this, the refutation of the reason follows.
A further argument is as follows: Even if this reason of "impermanence" is taken to be inconclusive because it shares common properties with both lightning and a jar, let us now ask:
Is sound established as being produced by immediate effort on account of its impermanence like that of a jar, or is it established as such on account of its impermanence like that of lightning?

If it were not produced by uninterrupted effort, then it would still apply to only one part of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and thus constitute the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

An example of that which applies to one part of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) while applying universally to the similar instances is as follows: when establishing the thesis that "sound is produced by uninterrupted effort."

Because it is produced by effort and exertion without interruption, the thesis [of sound] has "impermanence" as its property. This property of impermanence exists pervasively in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as jars and the like.
In the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), such as lightning and space, it exists partially—it exists in lightning and the like, but does not exist in space and the like.
Therefore, as before, this too is an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason.
This refers to the following formal argument: "Sound is the subject (dharmin); its being produced by immediate effort is the thesis (pakṣa);

the reason (hetu) is 'because it possesses the nature of impermanence'. Although this reason of "the nature of impermanence" occurs pervasively within the similar instances (sapakṣa), it still occurs partially within the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) and cannot be said not to occur there. Therefore, it is also termed "inconclusive" (anaikāntika).
This is not an error. For a thesis produced by diligent and uninterrupted effort must necessarily take jars and the like as its similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Now, the reason—its nature of impermanence—is present throughout these jars and the like; this is called "pervasion across all similar instances," and thus there is certainly no fault.
However, a thesis produced by diligent and uninterrupted effort must necessarily take lightning, space, and so forth as its dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). Now...
This reason for impermanence still exists in one portion of those [examples], such as lightning, while it is only in another portion, such as space, that it is absent.
Is it not the case, then, that the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) does not merely fail to apply to one portion, but actually applies to another portion?
To say, "Therefore, as before, this is also inconclusive" means that even if one were to argue as follows:
Regarding this nature of impermanence, if one takes lightning and a jar as the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), one should raise the following objection:
"Is it because of its impermanence like lightning that sound is established as not being produced immediately after volitional effort?
Or is it because of its impermanence like a jar that sound is established as being produced immediately after volitional effort? Thus, once again...
Likewise, if a reason occurs only in a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), it constitutes the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Regarding that which occurs in only a portion of both [similar and dissimilar] instances: for example, if one says, "Sound is eternal because it lacks material resistance (*amūrtatva*)," here the thesis (*pakṣa*) of eternity takes space (*ākāśa*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*) as its similar instances.
The property of lacking material resistance exists in space and so forth, but does not exist in atoms and so forth.
Taking things such as jars and pleasure (*sukha*) as the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*): [the reason] exists in pleasure and so forth, but does not exist in jars and so forth.

Therefore, because this reason shares the same property (*sādharmya*) with both pleasure and space (*ākāśa*), it is also called "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*). (The character for *le* [pleasure] is pronounced *luò*.)

"Partially occurring in both the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*. This means that it occurs in one part of the similar class and the dissimilar class, while not occurring in the other parts.
The preceding section explained the true probans (*saddhetu*), which must be "certainly present in the similar class" and "entirely absent from the dissimilar class.

"Certainly present" carries the sense of "pervasive occurrence," while "entirely absent" carries the sense of "non-occurrence. Now, if it only partially occurs in the similar class, it is not [a true probans].

It is necessarily present. If it were to occur in only one part of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), it would not be "universally absent. This means, for example, if one were to formulate a syllogism as follows:
"Sound" is the subject (*dharmin*); "necessarily eternal" is the thesis (*pakṣa*); "because it lacks material resistance" is the reason (*hetu*).
This reason of "lacking material resistance" occurs in only one part of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and cannot occur universally therein; yet it likewise [occurs] in the dissimilar instance.
Because it does not exist universally [in the similar instances], it is also called the "fallacy of the uncertain" (*anaikāntika*).
That is to say, in this context, the thesis of permanence must necessarily take space (*ākāśa*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth as its similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Now, this reason—being "without the nature of resistance"—exists in space and the like, but does not exist in atoms and the like; thus, it exists in only one part of the similar instances.
It shifts. Furthermore, this thesis of permanence must necessarily take things such as jars and pleasure (*sukha*) as dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

Now, this reason of "the nature of being non-obstructive" still exists in pleasure and the like, yet it does not exist in jars and the like; thus, it still occurs partially within the dissimilar instance.
The above constitutes the formal refutation. The following section refutes the shifting argument, namely, that this [reason of] being non-obstructive...
Regarding the reason of "nature": even if one were to claim that sound is [impermanent] because it shares the same property as pleasure and emptiness, this would still be called "inconclusive.
Now, let us pose this question: Is it like emptiness, which lacks substantial obstruction, that proves sound is permanent? Or is it like pleasure, which lacks substantial obstruction?

If, however, one intends to prove that sound is impermanent, then [the reason] would still apply only to a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and thus constitutes the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
As for the contradictory counter-probans (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*), it is as when one establishes the thesis: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar."

Some establish that sound is eternal because it possesses the nature of being audible, just like the nature of sound itself. Since both of these [reasons] are causes of doubt, they are both termed "inconclusive" (anaikāntika).
Regarding the thesis of impermanence: although it takes "being a product" as its reason, one cannot say that sound is not "audible";
thus, it would be unable to refute those who falsely imagine permanence and establish impermanence. Regarding the thesis of permanence:
although it takes "being audible" as its reason, one cannot say that sound is not "a product"; thus, it would be unable to refute impermanence.
They establish the thesis of permanence while speaking of what is correct; thus, although their positions are mutually contradictory, both remain wavering and uncertain.
Question: How can one refute their doctrine of permanence and establish impermanence? Answer: One should overturn their syllogism as follows: "The nature of sound is the subject (dharmin);
its thesis (pakṣa) is that it is definitely impermanent; the reason (hetu) is that it is admitted to be audible. This is the same [as the previous argument].
It is, for example, like the object of sound. Alternatively, it is said: "The sound that is heard" is the subject (*dharmin*); "it is definitely impermanent" is the thesis (*pakṣa*);

"because it is admitted to be something heard" is the reason (*hetu*); and "like the visible form that is seen" is the concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*). Regarding the second explanation, there are six types of inconclusive reasons (*anaikāntika*) concerning the six sense objects.
△ Third, the explanation of contradictory reasons (*viruddha*) has two parts: first, listing the names; second, explaining their characteristics. Now, the first part.

There are four types of contradiction: namely, the contradictory reason regarding the specific characteristic of the property (*dharma-svalakṣaṇa-viruddha-hetu*), the contradictory reason regarding the specific qualification of the property (*dharma-viśeṣa-viruddha-hetu*), the contradictory reason regarding the specific characteristic of the locus (*dharmin-svalakṣaṇa-viruddha-hetu*), and the contradictory reason regarding the specific qualification of the locus (*dharmin-viśeṣa-viruddha-hetu*), and so forth.

The self-characteristic of the property (*dharma*) is the verbal expression of the essence of the thesis; the differentiation of the property is the conceptual acceptance of the essence of the thesis.

The self-characteristic of the property-bearer (*dharmin*) is the verbal expression of the basis of the thesis; the differentiation of the property-bearer is the conceptual acceptance of the basis of the thesis.
△ Second, the explanation of the characteristics.

Among these, the reason that contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the thesis is as follows: for example, to say "Sound is permanent because it is produced," or "because it is produced immediately following an effort.
This reason exists only in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*); therefore, it is contradictory.
Sound is the subject (*dharmin*). "Necessarily eternal" is the thesis (*pakṣa*). "Eternity" is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property (*dharma*).

If one takes "being produced" as the reason (*hetu*), or "being produced by effort without interval" as the reason, these two reasons exist only in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) where the thesis is non-eternal;
therefore, they contradict the specific characteristic of the thesis of eternity.

Regarding the reason that contradicts the specific qualification of the thesis (*dharmaviśeṣaviruddhahetu*): for example, it is said that the eyes and so forth must exist for the sake of another because they possess a composite nature (*saṃghātatva*), like bedding and other such items.

While this reason can establish that the eyes and so forth must exist for the sake of another, it likewise establishes the opposite of the specific qualification of the thesis—that is, it establishes that the "other" for whom these composites exist is itself a composite, as in the case of bedding and other such things which exist for the sake of a composite.
Because it is that which is experienced.
Non-Buddhists take the conception of a self (*ātman*) as their fundamental tenet, and this self has two meanings:

first, the *puruṣa-ātman*, which is neither born nor extinguished, and is thus the essence of true permanence; second, the "self-body," which is formed by the accumulation of the four great elements and is subject to birth.
There is cessation; this is that which is experienced by the *puruṣa* (the self).

They claim that just as a collection of bedding and other such items must necessarily serve the needs of the body, so too must the collection of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that constitutes the body of the eyes and so forth necessarily be used by the *puruṣa*.
If there were no *puruṣa*, what need would there be for a body composed of the collection of the four great elements? For example, if...

Since there is no body composed of the accumulation of the four great elements, what need is there for bedding and other such items? Therefore, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established as follows: The subject (*dharmin*) is the eye and so forth;
the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they must be used by another, namely, a self (*ātman*). The reason (*hetu*) is that the eye and so forth possess the nature of being an accumulation.
The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like bedding and so forth, which, being accumulations, must necessarily be used by a body. Herein, "another" refers to...
The single character "self" (ātman) refers to the very essence of the doctrine they propound, which they designate as "dharma.

However, in relation to the eyes and so forth, the *puruṣa* (spiritual self) is considered "other"; yet, in relation to bedding and furniture, the body—which is an aggregate of the eyes and so forth—is again considered "other.
Thus, upon this single character "other," there are two distinct types of differentiation. Therefore, we now refute this as follows:
This is the reason for the nature of being an aggregate. Suppose it could be established that the eyes and so forth must necessarily be used by another, namely the self (*ātman*);

in that case, one could likewise establish that they are used by another in the sense of being an aggregate, which contradicts the specific characteristics of the thesis you yourself have established. Why? Because we observe that things such as bedding and the like are merely...
Because one accumulates things for the sake of others' enjoyment; since one has already accumulated bedding and requisites solely for the use of others, why then would one accumulate a body?

Furthermore, how could it necessarily be for the sake of a self (ātman)? Even if such a self did exist, since the self has no need for bedding, what need would it have for a body? Moreover, as for the accumulation of bedding and requisites—since...
If it is merely for the sake of the functioning of the accumulated body, then the accumulated body itself must also be merely for the sake of another accumulation.
If the *puruṣa* (Self) were also an accumulation, it would therefore be called "other" and would thus be impermanent, as well as not the true Self.
If the *puruṣa* were not an accumulation, then it ought not to employ the eyes and so forth, which are accumulations; for [it is] the accumulated body that...

Because one must experience accumulated objects, the three characters established therein refer to the very nature of the "proposition" (*pakṣa*) posited by the non-Buddhists—that it necessarily exists for the sake of another.
They wish to establish the *puruṣa* (Self) as that "other" which acts as the user, using the reason of "accumulated nature.
Now, by means of that very same reason of "accumulated nature," we instead establish the accumulation itself.

If one aggregates these [attributes] elsewhere and treats them as functional, then the "spiritual self" (śūnyātman) collapses without being attacked; therefore, this is called a "reason contradictory to the specific characteristics of the property" (*dharmaviśeṣaviruddha*).

An example of a reason contradictory to the specific characteristic of the subject (*dharmin-svarūpaviruddhahetu*) is: "Existence (*sattā*) is not a substance, not a quality, and not an activity; it possesses [existence]."
Because it is real, and because it possesses the activity of a quality, just like the property of "sameness-and-difference" (sāmānyaviśeṣa).
This reason, just as it can establish the negation of reality and so forth, can likewise establish the negation of existence (sattva), because both [premises] are certain.
The Vaiśeṣika school establishes six categories (padārtha): 1. The category of substance (dravya), which refers to the nine kinds beginning with earth. 2.
The category of quality (guṇa), which refers to the twenty-four kinds beginning with color. 3. The category of action (karma), which refers to the five kinds beginning with grasping. 4.

The category of great existence (mahāsattā), which refers to a distinct entity existing apart from substances, qualities, and actions; it is by virtue of this "great existence" that substances, qualities, and actions exist.

Therefore, "existence" (*sat*) refers to that which possesses the capacity for existence; "reality," "quality," and "activity" refer to that which is possessed. Regarding the five categories of "identity and difference":

it is by means of these categories that all phenomena are established as having their respective identities and differences. For example, when earth is compared to earth, there is the sense of identity;

when earth is compared to water and so forth, there is the sense of difference. This identity and difference of earth—namely, that it is earth and not water, and so forth—is [established through these categories].

It is likewise. One falsely imagines that these terms of identity and difference also possess a distinct intrinsic nature. Sixth is the term "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), which refers to a collection of dharmas.
By means of the term "conjunction," it is like a bird flying through the sky that suddenly reaches a tree branch and stays there, not departing.

Because of the category of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), there is the activity of persistence. Now, first we shall establish a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) based on their false conceptualization, and subsequently expose its fallacies.
First, the formal inference is established as follows: Thesis: That which is called "the nature of existence" (*mahāsattā*) is not a substance, nor a quality, nor an action.
Reason: Because it possesses substance, and because it possesses qualities and actions. Example: Just like the nature of "similarity and difference" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*).

Next, the rebuttal states: "The reasons 'because this possesses one reality' and 'because it possesses qualities and activities' are intended to establish that [the universal *mahāsāmānya*] exists by negating [its being] a substance (*dravya*) and so forth, and thus claim it is the nature of the Great Universal (*mahāsattā*), being neither substance, nor quality, nor activity.

However, in this same manner, one could also establish the negation of the nature of the Great Universal by claiming it is neither substance, nor quality, nor activity—and thus it would also not exist."

The nature of *mahāsattā* (Great Existence). Why? Because that which possesses real substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and activity (*karman*) is definitely not [itself] substance, quality, or activity;

therefore, that which possesses substance, quality, and activity is also definitely not the nature of *mahāsattā*. Since both are definitively so, one should state the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
That which you maintain to be the nature of *mahāsattā* is the subject (*dharmin*); since it is neither substance, nor quality, nor activity, it must also [be non-existent].

The thesis is not that [substance] has the nature of being great (*mahat*). The reason (*hetu*) is stated as: "because it possesses one real entity" and "because it possesses qualities and actions. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like [the case of] real entities, qualities, and actions.

A reason that contradicts the specific qualification of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviruddha-hetu*) is, for instance, this very same reason when applied to a specific qualification of the subject within the aforementioned thesis.

It establishes the nature of having a cause (*sopādānatva*), and is likewise able to establish its opposite, the nature of lacking a cause (*anupādānatva*), just as in the case of negating [the existence of] substance (*dravya*) and so forth, because both are equally certain.
This reason refers to the reasons "because there exists a single substance" and "because there exist qualities and actions. The subject (*dharmin*) of the preceding thesis—

Regarding "differentiation" (*viśeṣa*): although the preceding text explicitly clarifies only that the category of "existence" (*sattā*) is existent, the intended implication is that the categories of "substance" (*dravya*), "quality" (*guṇa*), and "action" (*karma*) are all likewise existent. Regarding "conditioning nature" (*pratyayatva*): this refers to the cause.

That is to say, for instance, the reasons given—namely, "because this substance exists" and "because quality and action exist"—are precisely what was previously negated as being non-substance, non-quality, and non-action.

This is the fundamental principle. Regarding the distinctions among phenomena, these may serve as the reasons for establishing them as having substantiality, possessing qualities, or performing functions;

yet they are likewise capable of establishing the opposite of these characteristics, serving as the reasons for establishing them as lacking substantiality, lacking qualities, or lacking functions. Why is this? For example, by means of this "existence of a substance,"...

Therefore, because there are qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karma*), and causes (*hetu*), one negates the existence of a "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*) that is neither quality, nor substance (*dravya*), nor action.
Furthermore, outside of the category of Great Existence, there must definitely exist separate categories of substance, quality, and action.

Moreover, by means of these very reasons—that because there is a single substance, there are qualities and actions—one establishes that outside of Great Existence, there definitely does not exist a separate category of substance.

Because both the categories of quality (*guṇa*) and action (*karman*) are determinate, the following formal inference (*bāhyamāna*) is stated therein: "The real (*dravya*), quality, and action are the subject (*dharmin*).

They are definitely distinct entities apart from the nature of 'Great Existence' (*mahāsattā*); this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because they possess one reality (*ekatva*), and because they possess qualities and actions.

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: like the nature of 'commonality and difference' (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*). To state a counter-inference (*pratikūlamāna*): those [entities] you maintain—the real, quality, and action—are the subject."

The thesis is that [the universal] "Great Existence" (mahāsattā) does not definitely exist apart from its own nature. The reason is: because it exists as a single substance, and because it possesses qualities and activities;
the example is like the nature of Great Existence itself. This concludes the four types of contradictory interpretations. The above clarifies the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
△ Section Three: Fallacious Similes (Dṛṣṭāntābhāsa). Part Two. First, the general heading; second, the detailed explanation. Now, the first [part].

Having already explained fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), the fallacious similes shall now be explained. There are five types of fallacious similes based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*): first, the unestablished property of the probans (*sādhanadharma-asiddha*); second, the unestablished property of the probandum (*sādhyadharma-asiddha*);

third, the unestablished of both; fourth, the lack of connection (*anupanaya*); and fifth, the inverted connection (*viparītopanaya*). [Next,] the fallacious similes based on difference (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).
The dharma and the analogy also have five types: first, the non-exclusion of the thesis; second, the non-exclusion of the probans; third, the non-exclusion of both;
fourth, non-separation; and fifth, inverted separation.
△ Second, the detailed explanation.
Regarding the "unestablished probans" (*asiddha-hetu*): for example, it is said that sound is permanent because it lacks resistance (*apratigha*).

One observes that all things lacking resistance are permanent, just like atoms (*paramāṇu*). However, in the case of those atoms, while the property to be established—permanence—is present, the [probans]...
To establish that there is no lack of material obstruction [in sound] is impossible, because all atoms possess the nature of material obstruction.

"That which establishes" (*sādhana*) is the reason (*hetu*); "that which is to be established" (*sādhya*) is the thesis (*pakṣa*). For example, if one were to say: "Sound is a phenomenon (*dharmin*); it is necessarily eternal (*nitya*), as its thesis.
The reason is stated: "Because it lacks material obstruction. The application (*upanaya*) is stated: "All things that lack material obstruction are seen to be eternal."

It is like an atom (*paramāṇu*). However, although that analogy of the atom may be granted as existing in respect to the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*), namely its permanence, it is nonetheless non-existent with respect to the property of the reason (*hetudharma*), namely its lack of resistance (*apratigha*). Why? Because all atoms...

Furthermore, because it possesses the nature of substantial resistance (*sapratighatva*), this constitutes a contradiction between the example and the reason; therefore, it is called "the unestablished nature of the property to be proven" (*sādhyadharmāsiddha*).

Regarding the "unestablished nature of the property to be proven," this refers to stating "like cognition" (*yathā buddhi*); however, in all cognitions, the property to be established lacks substantiality.
There is the property of resistance (*sapratighatva*), yet the property to be established—the permanence of sound—is absent, because all cognitions (*buddhi*) are impermanent.

This [argument] likewise takes the permanence of sound as the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the lack of material resistance (*amūrtatva*) as the reason (*hetu*), with cognition serving as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

However, although the lack of material resistance exists in the case of the reason-property (*hetudharma*) within all cognitions, it does not exist in the case of the thesis-property (*sādhyadharma*) of permanence.
The nature [of the example] does not exist. Why? Because all cognitions are impermanent. Thus, the example contradicts the thesis;
therefore, it is called "the unestablished nature of the property to be proven" (*sādhyadharmāsiddha*).
Regarding the failure of both [theses] to be established, there are two types: existence and non-existence. If one says "like a jar," it is not established for either existence or non-existence.
If one says "like space," it is not established for either non-existence or existence.
Both are unestablished; that is to say, there is the fault of non-establishment regarding both the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) and the reason (*hetu*).
This, moreover, is of two kinds. First, there is the case where the example exists, yet the example contradicts the thesis and the reason, and thus both are unestablished.
Second is the "non-existent example" (*abhāva-dṛṣṭānta*). Since the example is non-existent, it is insufficient to establish the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*);
