therefore, both fail. First, let us explain the existent example: if one says, "Sound is permanent because it lacks material resistance;

like a jar," although the jar exists, its nature is impermanent and it possesses material resistance; thus, both [the reason and the example] fail. Next, let us explain the non-existent [example]. If...
To say that sound is permanent because it lacks substantial obstruction, using space as an analogy, may be acceptable when addressed to those who maintain the existence of space.

However, if addressed to those who maintain the non-existence of space, then since space itself does not exist, how can one discuss whether it is permanent or impermanent, or obstructive or non-obstructive?
Therefore, [the argument] is likewise unestablished for both parties.
"Non-conjunction" means that there is no actual union at that location; rather, both the probans and the probandum appear together in relation to a jar or the like, as when one says:
"In the jar, one perceives both the property of being produced and the property of impermanence."

The "prover" (sādhana) is the reason (*hetu*), which here refers to the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*). The "probandum" (*sādhya*) is the thesis (*pakṣa*), which here refers to the property of impermanence (*anityatva*).
Logically, one ought to state: "All things that are produced are impermanent; the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is like a jar. Only by doing so can the meaning be fully revealed.
Since the application (*upanaya*) is now absent, the meaning is not revealed; therefore, this too constitutes a fault.

Regarding "inverted application" (viparyaya-yojanā): it refers to when one should say, "All conditioned things (saṃskṛta) are impermanent," yet instead says in reverse, "All impermanent things are conditioned."
Furthermore, there are cases where something is impermanent yet not produced; thus, the same fault is incurred.
This is called the "fallacious similar example" (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).
This concludes the summary that there are five types of fallacious similar examples.

Regarding the case where the probandum is not excluded within the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*): for instance, suppose someone says, "All impermanent things are seen to possess resistance, like atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Because that person posits atoms as being permanent, the property to be established—permanence—is not excluded [from the atoms];
however, the property that serves as the reason—the absence of resistance—is absent [in atoms].
In establishing a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), the primary purpose is fundamentally to provide a counter-illustration of the similar property (*sādharmya*).

Thus, if one wishes to use "impermanence" to counter-illustrate the thesis of "permanence," or "resistance" to counter-illustrate the reason of "non-resistance," one must establish a dissimilar example in order to thereby counter-illustrate the similar example.

For instance, in the case of one who establishes that sound is permanent, or again, as some might say: "All things that are impermanent are seen to possess resistance, just like [an object such as] a jar."
As for the atom (*paramāṇu*), this dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) does not exclude [the possibility of] the thesis (*sādhya*) of permanence;
for those non-Buddhists originally established that atoms are permanent, yet now they instead employ the atom as a dissimilar example, whereby the thesis would conversely become impermanent.

Thus, it is insufficient to manifest the thesis of permanence. Therefore, this dissimilar example of the minute particle (*rajas*) applies only to the reason of "lack of material obstruction" (*apratighāta*).

Thus, while [the property] is absent [in the example], it still exists within the constant subject (*pakṣa*). This constitutes a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) that is established for the reason (*hetu*), yet not established for the subject;
this is termed "the non-exclusion of the thesis" (*asādhyavyāvṛtti*).
Regarding "not refuting the probans": this refers to stating that it is like [the case of] karma; one merely refutes the probandum (sādhya) without refuting the probans (sādhana).
For they claim that all karmas lack material resistance (sapratigha).

That is to say, if one establishes that sound is permanent and provides a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) such as "action" (karman), this merely negates the thesis to be established—the permanence of sound—but does not negate the probans—the reason of being non-obstructive. This is because it is asserted that all actions are non-obstructive.
Thus, while it serves as a dissimilar example for the thesis, it fails to serve as a dissimilar example for the reason; this is termed "the failure of the probans to exclude [the counter-instance]."
Regarding "neither being negated": this refers to the proponents of existence (astivādin) who assert that [space] is like empty space.

This is because they do not negate the nature of permanence and lack of material obstruction (apratigha) in that empty space, as they maintain that empty space is permanent by nature and lacks material obstruction.

This means that if one who does not accept the existence of space were to establish the thesis that sound is permanent, and were to cite "space" as a dissimilar example (vipakṣa), then for someone who accepts the existence of space, those two characters "space" would be unable to exclude the thesis of permanence, nor would they be able to exclude the reason of "lack of material obstruction.
Since it fails entirely to function as a dissimilar example, it is called "failing to exclude both. Why?
Therefore, because their treatise on space asserts that space is of a permanent nature and is devoid of material obstruction, [the opponent] does not concede it;
that is to say, they claim that just as with a jar, one perceives impermanence and the quality of material obstruction.
This means that when those who establish the thesis of permanence merely state the dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta), saying, "For instance,

a jar is seen to have the nature of impermanence and the nature of being obstructive," but do not state, "All things that are impermanent are seen to be obstructive, just like jars and so forth," then the principle of exclusion (vyatireka) is not manifested;
therefore, it is called "non-exclusion" (avyatireka).
Regarding "inverted exclusion" (*viparīta-vyatireka*): it refers, for example, to saying, "All that is substantially obstructive is impermanent.

If one is establishing the thesis of impermanence, the correct formulation of the concordant example (*sapakṣa*) should be stated as: "In all that is substantially obstructive, one observes its impermanence."
It is like the example of a jar and so forth. Now, in establishing the thesis of permanence, the dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*) must be stated separately;

thus one should say: "All things that are impermanent are observed to possess material obstruction. Only then will it not be erroneous. For instance, if one were to say, "All things that possess material obstruction are impermanent," this would be called an erroneous separation (*viparyasta-vyatireka*).

Generally, in a positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the reason (*hetu*) must come first and the thesis (*pakṣa*) afterwards; in a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the thesis must necessarily come first and the reason afterwards.
The logical sequence (*vākya-krama*) must be thus; it must certainly not be disordered. If it is disordered, it is not a genuine *sādhana*.
The first part, the formal explanation within the second section on "Fallacious *Sādhanas*," is hereby concluded. △ Second, the summary of the faults.
Statements such as these, which resemble the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*), are not authentic means of proof.
This concludes the second section: the two gates of pseudo-means of proof. △ Third, the two gates of true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and true inference (*anumāna*).
This is divided into three parts: first, the general heading; second, the detailed explanation; third, the summary. Now, the first part: the general heading.
Furthermore, for the sake of one's own awakening, one should know that there are only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
II. Detailed Explanation.
Among these, direct perception refers to non-conceptualization. If there is correct cognition regarding objects such as form (*rūpa*), it is free from names, categories (*jāti*), and so forth.
All conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) operate distinctly as they manifest; therefore, it is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). "Manifest" (*pratyakṣa*) means appearing clearly and distinctly.
"Perception" (*pramāṇa*) means measurement and definitive determination. Regarding "non-conceptual": there are three types of conceptual construction:

first, conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*); second, conceptualization following recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*); and third, conceptualization through deliberation (*abhinirūpaṇa-vikalpa*).

Now, when it is devoid of the two kinds of conceptualization—recollection and deliberation—it is termed "manifest. When there is only self-nature conceptualization, it is termed "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*).
This self-nature conceptualization is itself non-conceptual; it does not mean that it is like earth, wood, stone, or metal. The *Awakening of Mahāśūnyatā Sūtra* says:
"For example, it is like the light of the eye clearly perceiving objects before it; that light is perfectly full and complete..."
There is neither aversion nor attachment. To clearly comprehend the objects before one is precisely the self-nature’s discrimination, which is itself right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*).
When one attains freedom from aversion and attachment, there is no longer discursive recollection or conceptualization; this is non-discrimination (*avikalpa*).

Generally speaking, that which is subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—namely, the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) realizing the principle of *tathatā* (suchness)—is correctly termed direct perception. This refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.

Taking the objects of the three types of natures as its domain is also called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The first five consciousnesses and the simultaneous mental consciousness taking present objects as their domain are also called direct perception.
The independent mental consciousness within meditative concentration taking the objects of dhyāna as its domain is also called direct perception.
When such a mind-king (*citta*) is in the state of direct perception, all associated mental factors (*caitta*) are likewise termed direct perception.

Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, the self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of all mind-kings (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*), which takes the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*) as its object, is also termed direct perception.
The self-witnessing-of-self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvittisaṃvittibhāga*) and the self-witnessing portion take each other as objects; these too are collectively designated as direct perception.
Therefore, this direct perception of correct cognition has never been absent, even for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who are deluded, confused, and mired in ignorance.

It is not that they are absent; it is simply that one is unaware of them during daily life. For now, let us examine their characteristics by means of the first five consciousnesses and the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Thus it is said: "If there is correct wisdom regarding the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena..."
It is free from the two kinds of conceptualization—namely, false recollection and discursive estimation—which arise from the seeds of linguistic habitual tendencies.
Each manifests distinctly with respect to its own specific objective aspect; therefore, it is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

As for the objects such as form and so forth, the six sense-fields are originally the self-transformed appearances of the six consciousnesses; they are not dharmas external to the mind, being without intrinsic nature and without arising.

It does not belong to the realm of verbal designation. Regarding the phrase "manifestations arise distinctly," this means that the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) manifests as clear discernment, while the *nimitta-bhāga* (object-aspect) manifests as a transformation;
these are merely of the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and do not fall under the delusions of pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpita*).
Therefore, they are termed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* asks: "External objects such as form are clearly perceived through direct perception."
"How can what has been attained be dismissed as non-existent? He replied: "When it is realized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), one does not grasp it as external.

It is only later that the conceptualizing mind falsely gives rise to the notion of externality. Thus, an ancient said: "Seeing forms and hearing sounds may occur but once. Furthermore, there is a verse that says:
"An immortal appears amidst clouds of colored light, holding a red silk fan to shield his face; you must quickly apply [the remedy]."
Look at the seer; do not look at the fan in the seer’s hand. How profound these words!
Regarding "inference" (anumāna), it means observing an object through its various characteristics (liṅga). As previously stated, there are three types of such characteristics.
With that as its cause, there arises a correct cognition regarding the object of inference, such as the knowledge that "there is fire" or "it is impermanent," etc.;
this is called inference (*anumāna*).

There are three types of marks (*liṅga*). These are the three characteristics within the reason (*hetu*) that avoid the fourteen fallacies. Because one perceives smoke as the reason, one understands that fire exists;
this serves as an analogy for perceiving the "produced" (*kṛtaka*) as the reason to know that phenomena (*dharma*) are impermanent (*anitya*).

Although this is not yet a direct realization (*pratyakṣa*), it is not erroneous regarding the meaning of the object under investigation; therefore, it is called inference (*anumāna*). It is precisely for this reason that the title is given as *Hetuvidyā* (The Science of Reason). Only...
Regarding those who receive the orthodox teaching: there are cases where the sixth consciousness is associated with correct understanding (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) and other mental factors (*caitta*).
△ Third, the summary:

Within the two types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that which is wisdom is called the "result" (*phala*), because it is the characteristic of realization and because it manifests as having a functional activity.
It is also called "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*).

Within these two types of valid cognition—direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*)—that which is non-conceptual correct knowledge (*nirvikalpa-samyagjñāna*) in direct perception, and that which is conceptual correct knowledge (*savikalpa-samyagjñāna*) produced by inference, are termed the "result" (*phala*). This is because direct perception is the means of realizing the characteristic [of the object]. Because...
Although inference (*anumāna*) has not yet been directly realized, it is also called a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it manifests as having a functional efficacy.
4. The Section on Fallacious Direct Perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*):

Discriminative cognition that operates in a manner different from the actual object is called fallacious direct perception. This refers to various cognitions that apprehend things such as jars or garments.

They arise from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Because they do not take the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of an object as their objective domain, they are called "pseudo-perception" (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).
Ordinary people see various conventional objects such as jars and garments and falsely claim that these too are perceptions;
in reality, they all arise from conceptual construction. This is because their conceptualizing cognition cannot apprehend the specific characteristic of objects such as form (*rūpa*).
These are merely different modes of conceptualizing objects; they do not correspond to what was previously described as "the manifestation of manifestations arising separately.
Therefore, they are termed "pseudo-direct perception" (*pratyakṣābhāsa*). △ Fifth, the section on pseudo-inference (*anumānābhāsa*).
If various cognitions of pseudo-objects arise preceded by a cognition of a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*), they are called pseudo-inference (*tarkābhāsa*).

As previously stated, there are many types of pseudo-reasons; when these are employed as causes, cognitions arise regarding pseudo-objects of inference that are unable to provide correct understanding.
This is called "pseudo-inference" (*anumānābhāsa*).

That is to say, when preceded by the cognition of a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*) that possesses fourteen fallacies, the various cognitions of pseudo-objects arising from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) are unable to provide correct understanding; therefore, they are termed pseudo-inference. There are ten types of pseudo-reasons.
If one commits even a single transgression among these four faults, the wisdom produced will not comprehend the correct meaning; it is therefore not authentic wisdom.

△ Section Seven: The Gate of Fallacious Refutations (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*).
If one expresses words that falsely point out a fault in a proof (*sādhana*), this is called a "pseudo-refutation" (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*).

That is to say: to point out a deficiency in a complete proof; to speak of a faulty thesis (*pakṣa*) when it is faultless; to speak of an unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*) when the reason is established;

to speak of an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*) when the reason is conclusive; to speak of a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*) when the reason is non-contradictory; [and to speak of a faulty proof] when it is faultless.

Regarding the example: there is a fallacious example (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa) consisting of faulty language; such speech is called a "pseudo-refutation" because it cannot reveal the faults of the opponent's position, as that [position] is without fault. Let us now leave this matter aside.
This clarifies that what appears to be a refutation cannot actually refute a genuine proof.

Having briefly proclaimed the meaning of a few phrases, I have established the initial directions; the principles of what is rational and irrational therein shall be skillfully debated elsewhere.
Upon first entering the Buddha-dharma, one must immediately use these few words and meanings to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox;
thus, they are established at the outset as the cardinal points. For example, when sailing upon the ocean, one requires a south-pointing chariot (*shinan che*) to recognize the directions.

Likewise, those who first wander the ocean of the Buddha-dharma require this *hetuvidyā* (logic) to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox. Truly, it is capable of establishing the real and manifesting direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Valid inference (*samyag-anumāna*) is called "reason" (*yukti*). That which resembles a valid proof (*sādhanābhāsa*), that which resembles direct perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*), and that which resembles valid inference (*anumānābhāsa*) are called "non-reason" (*ayukti*).
Non-reason can be refuted; reason cannot be refuted. All scriptural collections (*śāstrapiṭaka*) do not go beyond the deliberation of this reason and non-reason;
therefore, it is said that "wondrous deliberation [is found] elsewhere. Thus, without studying *hetuvidyā* (logic), there is no way to enter [this deliberation].
Without exhausting the ocean of the teachings through the gateway of Right Reasoning (*nyāya*), one cannot fully exhaust the subtleties of Hetuvidyā (Logic).
